title: Motor compensation and its effects on neural reorganization after stroke

authors.name: Theresa A. Jones
authors.affiliation: The University of Texas at Austin

abstract: Stroke instigates a dynamic process of repair and remodelling of remaining neural circuits, and this process is shaped by behavioural experiences. The onset of motor disability simultaneously creates a powerful incentive to develop new, compensatory ways of performing daily activities. Compensatory movement strategies that are developed in response to motor impairments can be a dominant force in shaping post-stroke neural remodelling responses and can have mixed effects on functional outcome. The possibility of selectively harnessing the effects of compensatory behaviour on neural reorganization is still an insufficiently explored route for optimizing functional outcome after stroke.

narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2017 review has achieved clear scholarly uptake in stroke rehabilitation and motor control, with 389 citations and field-normalized standing in the top 10% for its year. Its influence is visible not only in journal articles, but also in preprints, conference papers, book chapters, dissertations, and methods-oriented work that engages compensatory movement, measurement, and recovery after stroke.

Full narrative

Theresa A. Jones’s review has become a well-cited reference point for understanding how compensatory movement strategies shape neural reorganization after stroke. The citation record shows sustained and broad academic use across the years, with especially strong uptake in rehabilitation, motor control, electromyography, transcranial magnetic stimulation, gait, and related measurement-focused subfields. The pattern suggests that the article is being used as both a conceptual framework and a practical guide for interpreting recovery trajectories.

The downstream literature reflects that breadth. The most visible citing venues include Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation, Neurorehabilitation and Neural Repair, IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering, Sensors, and several preprint servers, indicating that the review informs both established clinical-neuroscience audiences and newer technology-enabled rehabilitation research. Recent citing works continue to extend its themes into sensor-based assessment, compensatory movement detection, daily arm-use quantification, and longitudinal stroke recovery studies.

The scite record is consistent with active scholarly engagement: most citation statements are neutral mentions, but there are supporting statements as well as a small number of contradictory ones, which is typical of a paper that has shaped an ongoing methodological and conceptual debate. In other words, the article is not merely cited as background; it is being read against, built upon, and refined as the field argues over when compensation helps recovery and when it may mask or limit neural change.

Beyond citations, the article shows documented reuse in 394 downstream works and is open through a green-access record with one open instance indexed. There are also a small number of public-facing mentions, including podcast appearances connected to the author and the topic area, but the dominant story remains scholarly: this is a highly visible review that has helped define how researchers think about compensation, rehabilitation, and post-stroke neural remodeling.
